title: Hidden will
hook: the Izbicer taught that God's will can hide inside human choices

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kotzker rebbe and his demand for truth with no comfort added. Your line was truth, fiercely. Were you honest about one thing? Today, a voice that came out of that same fierce room. Day one thousand two hundred two.

Joseph's brothers stand in front of him in Egypt, terrified. Years before, they threw him in a pit and sold him. Now he rules the country's grain, and they need bread. He could punish them. Instead he says something strange. "So now it was not you that sent me hither, but God." Not you. They did it. They remember doing it. And Joseph tells them a second story was running underneath their story the whole time. One teacher in the Hasidic world pressed that idea into places that still unsettle his readers. Today's word is his.
screen: `THE BROTHERS IN EGYPT.` → `IT WAS NOT YOU, BUT GOD.` → `A STORY UNDER THE STORY.`

segments.voice: Hidden will. The teacher is Rabbi Mordechai Yosef Leiner, called the Izbicer after his town, Izbica. Tradition says he learned in the Kotzker's circle before going his own way. His teachings were gathered in a book called Mei HaShiloach, the waters of Shiloah. Turn his idea four ways. First, the old line. The Talmud says everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven. So a person's choice to stand in awe of God is their own. Second, the Izbicer's push. In his readings, even our choices can carry God's will inside them, hidden. A person acts, sure that they are acting alone, and later it turns out that something larger was moving through the act. Joseph saw it in his brothers: "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good." Third, the hard part. The Izbicer reads some uncomfortable stories this way, people in the Torah who seem to break the rules, and asks whether a deeper will was at work. Readers argue over these passages; some find them daring, some unsettling. Fourth, the guardrail. The Izbicer did not tell people to drop the commandments and follow their urges. In ordinary life, his readers say, a person walks by the law. The hidden will is something you might glimpse, if at all, looking back. Which brings it to an ordinary Tuesday. You cannot see the whole of your own story from inside it. A wrong turn, a closed door, a person who hurt you. The Izbicer doesn't say the hurt was good. He says the last word on what it meant may not be yours to write yet.
screen: `THE IZBICER AND HIS BOOK.` · `IN THE HANDS OF HEAVEN.` · `GOD'S WILL INSIDE OUR CHOICES.` · `SEEN, IF AT ALL, LOOKING BACK.` · then, large: `HIDDEN WILL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept one mystery. Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind one thing in your life you don't understand. Not a crisis. Something that happened and still doesn't make sense: a plan that fell apart, a meeting you didn't expect. Hold it gently. You don't have to explain it, and you don't have to call it good. Just let it stay a question. On each breath out, loosen your grip on needing the answer today. If you pray, you can hold it there, in the hands of Heaven. The bell holds the time.
Hidden will. The Izbicer's teaching that God's will can hide inside human choices, seen, if at all, only looking back, while ordinary life still walks by the law. Today's word.
Your line: hidden will. Today, when something goes sideways, try saying only this: I don't know yet what this is. Then carry on. Day one thousand two hundred two.

howItsDone: Students of the Izbicer read Mei HaShiloach slowly, often with a teacher, alongside the weekly Torah portion, and his teachings are discussed in Hasidic and other study circles as a way to think about choice and providence.
